Compared to literature
Hamstring muscle activity during high-speed running was previously assessed with multichannel
EMG for the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus.23,25 These two studies investigated primarily
the effect of running speed on the amplitude of normalized muscle activity within each muscle.23,25 One
of these studies reported within hamstring muscle activity distribution as a sub-analysis.25 In contrast to
our findings, no differences were found among three regions within the biceps femoris long head and
semitendinosus, when comparing muscle activity over a stride cycle during high-speed running.25 One of
multiple possible explanations is that heterogeneous activity was possibly averaged out in the
aforementioned study, as means were calculated over multiple EMG channels to form three regions per
muscle. Our results indicate heterogeneous muscle activity within the hamstring muscles if assessed
using a configuration with multiple regions during high-speed running. There was also a difference in
what MVIC was used for normalization of the signal, which probably resulted in lower normalized EMG
activity in our study. The maximum value of a single sample was used in our study probably resulted in a
relatively lower normalized EMG activity (Figure 2 & 3) compared to an averaged value over a 1-s epoch
in the aforementioned study.25 For comparisons between muscles, existing literature is limited to single
channel EMG studies.28,39,40 None of these studies evaluated the semimembranosus activity.28,39,40 In the
early-swing phase, studies described a significantly higher muscle activity in the semitendinosus
compared to the biceps femoris long, which is in contrast to our results.28,39,40 A possible explanation can
be the heterogeneous activity distribution within the individual hamstring muscles. We measured higher
normalized muscle activity in the proximal and distal regions of the biceps femoris long head during the
early-swing phase compared to the middle electrode location, which roughly corresponds to the
electrode location used in the aforementioned studies.28,39,40 In the late-swing phase, no significant
differences between the muscle activity of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus during
high-speed running were reported, which is in line with our results.28,39,40 An interesting observation in
our results was the decrease of mean normalized muscle activity of all three hamstring muscles just
before heel-strike, at the end of the late-swing phase (Figure 3). Here, the semitendinosus and
semimembranosus activity decreased rapidly, while the biceps femoris long head remained more active
into the stance phase. This effect was statistically significant when comparing relative contributions
between muscles (Figure 4), yet not when looking at normalized muscle activity (Figure 3). The higher
contribution of the biceps femoris long head in the late-swing phase was possibly again caused by the
heterogeneous activity of this muscle. The most proximal electrode location showed again significantly
higher normalized muscle activity in the late-swing phase compared to the two distal electrode location.
This proximal location corresponds to the most frequently injured location within the biceps femoris
long head.41,42 This is also the phase during high-speed running and location within the biceps femoris
long head with the highest strain according to model studies.43,44 It would be interesting to examine
neural drive between the hamstring muscles in the late-swing phase during high-speed running and the
relationship between activity levels in the proximal region of the biceps femoris long head and injury
occurrence.45,46
Hip and knee joint angles at peak EMG activity for different electrode location did not differ
significantly. All peak EMG activities, both within individual muscles as well as over the mean of each of
the muscles, occurred in the late-swing phase. These results corresponds to results of a previous study
in which the peak EMG activity was compared between sprinting and a variety of hamstring exercises for
individual hamstring muscles.27 The reported hip and joint angles at peak EMG activity of the biceps
femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus were within one standard deviation of our
results.27 All peak EMG activities occurred at high musculotendinous length, when the hamstring
muscles perform the largest amount of negative work.6 This indicates that high muscle activity, muscle
strain and negative power coincide and may explain why the late-swing phase is associated with
hamstring injury occurrence.
The strength of this study is the use of multichannel EMG, compared to single electrode usage.
It has previously been shown that heterogeneous muscle activity can cause an over- or underestimation
when using conventional single-channel EMG recordings.24,26 To highlight the importance, we repeated
the between hamstring analyses with the electrode location per muscle which corresponded most to
the SENIAM guidelines.30 As a result, the between-muscle difference in normalized muscle activity in the
late-swing phase disappeared (see Supplementary Figure 13). This observation, especially because it
appears in the late-swing phase, signifies the additional value of using multiple EMG channels per
muscle. Future studies should confirm this by comparing multichannel EMG with SENIAM guidelines.
Limitations
One of the limitations of this study is that inclusion was restricted to uninjured basketball players, which
might limit generalizability to other and injured athletes. Furthermore, an inherent limitation of using
EMG is cross-talk between muscles. With multichannel EMG, electrode locations are closer to proximal
and distal muscle borders compared to conventional EMG, which may be more prone to crosstalk. Given
the expertise in clinical care and based on comparisons with MRI in the larger RCT, manual palpation
was considered accurate for identifying hamstring muscles. By careful electrode placement over the
targeted muscle belly, minimizing inter-electrode to 22 mm and using differential amplification, cross-
talk and electrode placement over tendon was minimized as much as possible, but cannot be completely
ruled out. It is furthermore unknown to what extent the influence is of the tendinous inscription within
the semitendinosus and electrode displacement by skin displacement because of movement.47 Future
studies should consider obtaining multiple MVIC values for normalization over a variety of hip and knee
joint angles, as a single MVIC can result in a fractional under- or overestimation of normalized muscle
activity.48 The approximately 4 kg extra weight of the safety harness and EMG registration device,
attached on the backside of the harness, had an unknown effect on the posture of the participants
during high-speed running. We did not exclude the participants with a history of a hamstring injury,
older than 12 months, or participants who had a history of ACL reconstruction with semitendinosus
tendon graft. They might have long-lasting effects on hamstring muscle activity and should be
considered when assessing unilateral muscle activity.49-52 Finally, participants were tested on a treadmill
and not in overground running to allow data acquisition. Treadmill-based running analysis is comparable
to over ground running and had as benefit that running speed can be regulated effectively.53
Conclusion
This study comprehensively described the distribution of hamstring muscle activity during high-speed
running, both within and between muscles. Our findings were that (i) when the hamstring muscles were
most active during high-speed running, in the late-swing phase, the semimembranosus was most active,
(ii) contrasting, the semitendinosus was least active in the late-swing phase during high-speed running,
(iii) within the biceps femoris long head, the most proximal region was significantly more active in the
late-swing phase, compared to other muscle regions, and (iv) peak muscle activity, assessed locally
within individual hamstring muscles, as well as in general over the whole muscle, occurred at similar hip
and knee joint angles during high-speed running.
Perspective
The present study provides novel information about the distribution of muscle activity of the hamstring
muscles during high-speed running. This comprehensive study showed that when the hamstring muscles
are most active, in the late-swing phase, the level of muscle activity of the semimembranosus is
significantly higher compared to the semitendinosus. Also in the late-swing phase during high-speed
running, the level of muscle activity in the most proximal part of the biceps femoris long head was
significantly more active compared to other regions within the same muscle. This location within the
biceps femoris long head corresponds to the most injurious area of the hamstring muscle. Peaks in
muscle activity occurred at similar hip and knee joint angles during high-speed running. Future studies
should examine if preventive interventions have an effect on the activity distribution during high-speed
running.
STATEMENTS & DECLARATIONS

The authors would like to thank LB Gerritsen for contribution in data collection, Dr. GS Faber for his
contribution to the measurement setup, Dr. SM Bruijn for his contribution to the data analysis and all

This trial was prospectively registered in the Netherlands Trial Register (date of registration 2018-07-13,

   "doi":"10.1111/sms.14326",
   "abstract":"Purpose: to assess activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running, comparing within and between muscle activity, relative contribution, and hip and knee angles at peak activity. Methods: multichannel EMG of male basketball players on a treadmill at 15 locations (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus). Results: 29 non-injured players (mean age 17 years). Heterogeneous activity was found within every hamstring muscle; in late swing, semimembranosus activity and relative contribution were higher than semitendinosus. Hip and knee angles at peak activity did not differ. Conclusion: hamstrings were most active in late swing, with the semimembranosus most active and the semitendinosus least active; the most proximal biceps femoris long head region was more active in late swing, and peak activity occurred at similar joint angles.",
   "tldr":"In uninjured male basketball players sprinting on a treadmill, hamstring activity was uneven within each muscle, peaked in late swing, and was lowest in the semitendinosus. Use this as a description of normal activation, not a measure of injury risk.",

Motion capture (100 Hz) defined early-swing, late-swing and stance phases in three strides at the highest maintained treadmill speed. Activity was tested with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping and repeated-measures ANOVA, and joint angles at peak activity with repeated-measures ANOVA.",
   "findings":"Of 38 participants tested, 29 were analysed. Within biceps femoris long head, the most proximal electrode had higher activity than all other locations (F(4,112) = 4.68). Between muscles, semitendinosus was lower than biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus in early swing and lower than semimembranosus in late swing (F(2,56) = 7.31). Relative contribution of semitendinosus was lower than the other two muscles in early and late swing (F(2,56) = 7.28). All peak activity occurred in late swing at mean hip 65.4 degrees and knee 57.3 degrees, with no significant differences in joint angle between muscles or locations.",
   "limitations":"Only uninjured players were tested, so findings may not transfer to injured athletes, and two participants had prior ACL injuries (one with semitendinosus graft). Surface EMG cross-talk cannot be fully excluded, a single MVIC was used for normalization, and the harness and recording device added about 4 kg. Treadmill running was used, and the abstract's late-swing relative-contribution result is worded differently from the Results, which report lower semitendinosus contribution in both swing phases. The PDF prints no journal name or issue year, so 2023 comes from the Crossref record and the download stamp.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff screening or rehabilitating hamstrings may note that late swing is the phase of highest activity in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, and that the proximal biceps femoris long head is most active there.    "athleteDev":"Limited.    "rtp":"Limited.  "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Training & Performance","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport","Track & Field","Soccer","Basketball","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified","Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Healthy Athletes","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A narrative review of acupuncture and dry needling for sports performance and recovery, drawing on RCTs, case reports and a systematic review of case reports, plus one meta-analysis of six RCTs with 210 participants on delayed-onset muscle soreness. The authors report mixed evidence that needling improves strength, power and flexibility, little evidence for endurance, and a pooled reduction in soreness, creatine kinase and strength loss after exercise. They conclude that needling is safe when performed by qualified practitioners but that higher quality studies are needed.",
 "screeningLimitations":"No search strategy is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked, and much of the performance evidence comes from small, single-session trials in healthy adults or students. Many cited sources are case reports or uncontrolled studies, and the authors state that the evidence base is not yet strong enough for specific recommendations.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may treat needling as an ergogenic aid or as a proven way to speed return to play, when the performance evidence is small and mixed, the recovery evidence is limited to soreness, and the return-to-play evidence is case-based.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Tang CT, Song B. Acupuncture and Dry Needling for Sports Performance and Recovery. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2022;21(6):213-218.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000000968",
   "abstract":"Acupuncture and dry needling share mechanisms and sports medicine applications. Pain is the most common indication, but there are limited studies on ergogenic use. Needling may improve muscular strength and power, including jump height, and flexibility. For recovery, acupuncture can relieve pain after injury and may help delayed-onset muscle soreness. There are many case reports in athletes, but more high-quality studies are needed for specific evidence-based recommendations. Given the high safety and few adverse events, needling can likely be promoted in athletes.",
   "tldr":"Needling has a good safety record in athletes and may help soreness and flexibility, but the evidence for strength and power gains is small and mixed, and the review finds no clear aerobic benefit. Use it as a low-risk adjunct, not a proven performance aid.",
   "methods":"A narrative review by two physicians in physical medicine and rehabilitation, summarizing acupuncture and dry needling research on performance (strength, power, endurance, flexibility) and recovery (muscle soreness). The article describes proposed mechanisms, cites randomized trials, case series, a systematic review of case reports in athletes, and a meta-analysis of DOMS trials, and includes perceptual interview data from track and field athletes. No search method is described.",
   "findings":"Most studies reported immediate strength or torque gains after acupuncture, with sham-controlled RCTs showing a difference when sham was non-penetrating (for example, average max torque and power in 20 healthy men and 32 female students). Dry needling produced no change in isometric strength in one study, and some vertical jump gains were short-lived. A meta-analysis of six RCTs (210 participants) found acupuncture reduced soreness (SMD -0.49), creatine kinase (SMD -0.91) and strength loss (SMD -0.54) after intense exercise. In a crossover study of 12 Paralympic powerlifters, dry needling and cold water immersion both raised IL-2 more at 24 to 48 h than at 2 to 24 h, and a marathon RCT found no reduction in cramping after dry needling.",
   "limitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and it draws on small single-session trials, case reports and sham controls of varying quality. The authors note that needling effects are partly nonspecific and that mechanisms are largely theoretical. Some cited studies had no control group, and the Lee et al. systematic review covered case reports only.",
   "practicalImplications":"Needling can be considered as a low-risk adjunct for soreness after training or competition, where the meta-analysis suggests a modest reduction, and for short-term range of motion before testing. It is not supported as a training method to raise strength or power, and the marathon study did not show that needling prevented cramps.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the evidence for strength, power and endurance gains is small, short-term and mixed. Torque or force gains were seen right after single sessions in healthy adults or students, and aerobic benefits are not convincing. Staff should not plan needling as a training stimulus on this evidence.",
   "rtp":"Limited. The review includes injured athletes and case reports of pain relief, but the return-to-play evidence is case-based or from small trials without standard return-to-sport criteria. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or to show that needling speeds return to sport, although athletes in one interview study valued the possibility of a quicker return."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"A narrative review of acupuncture and dry needling for sports performance and recovery, drawing on RCTs, case reports and a systematic review of case reports, plus one meta-analysis of six RCTs with 210 participants on delayed-onset muscle soreness.  "synthesisCaution":"Staff may treat needling as an ergogenic aid or as a proven way to speed return to play, when the performance evidence is small and mixed, the recovery evidence is limited to soreness, and the return-to-play evidence is case-based.",

   "abstract":"Acupuncture and dry needling share mechanisms and sports medicine applications. Pain is the most common indication, but there are limited studies on ergogenic use. Needling may improve muscular strength and power, including jump height, and flexibility. For recovery, acupuncture can relieve pain after injury and may help delayed-onset muscle soreness. There are many case reports in athletes, but more high-quality studies are needed for specific evidence-based recommendations. Given the high safety and few adverse events, needling can likely be promoted in athletes.",
   "tldr":"Needling has a good safety record in athletes and may help soreness and flexibility, but the evidence for strength and power gains is small and mixed, and the review finds no clear aerobic benefit. Use it as a low-risk adjunct, not a proven performance aid.",
   "methods":"A narrative review by two physicians in physical medicine and rehabilitation, summarizing acupuncture and dry needling research on performance (strength, power, endurance, flexibility) and recovery (muscle soreness). The article describes proposed mechanisms, cites randomized trials, case series, a systematic review of case reports in athletes, and a meta-analysis of DOMS trials, and includes perceptual interview data from track and field athletes. No search method is described.",
   "findings":"Most studies reported immediate strength or torque gains after acupuncture, with sham-controlled RCTs showing a difference when sham was non-penetrating (for example, average max torque and power in 20 healthy men and 32 female students). Dry needling produced no change in isometric strength in one study, and some vertical jump gains were short-lived. A meta-analysis of six RCTs (210 participants) found acupuncture reduced soreness (SMD -0.49), creatine kinase (SMD -0.91) and strength loss (SMD -0.54) after intense exercise. In a crossover study of 12 Paralympic powerlifters, dry needling and cold water immersion both raised IL-2 more at 24 to 48 h than at 2 to 24 h, and a marathon RCT found no reduction in cramping after dry needling.",
   "limitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and it draws on small single-session trials, case reports and sham controls of varying quality. The authors note that needling effects are partly nonspecific and that mechanisms are largely theoretical. Some cited studies had no control group, and the Lee et al. systematic review covered case reports only.",

   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the evidence for strength, power and endurance gains is small, short-term and mixed.  "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Training & Performance","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Rehabilitation","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A narrative overview of blood flow restriction (BFR) physiology, cuff and pressure selection, alternative uses and contraindications, drawing on RCTs, meta-analyses and safety studies in rehabilitation, training and older adults. The authors report that low-load BFR (about 30% of 1RM) produces hypertrophy and strength gains, that it gives smaller strength gains than heavy loading, and that VTE and muscle damage risks appear low when protocols are screened and submaximal. They conclude BFR is generally safe and useful in rehabilitation, with more research needed on mechanisms and protocols.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The paper describes no search strategy, and most cited evidence comes from patients, older adults or healthy adults rather than athletes; athlete-specific content is limited to a sentence on aerobic BFR for elite athletes. The safety conclusions rest on incidence figures from Japan and small studies that the authors note disagree about rhabdomyolysis risk.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may read BFR as safe for any athlete at any load, or as equal to heavy resistance training for strength, when the review shows smaller strength gains than heavy loading and safety depends on screening, cuff choice and avoiding failure.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Martin PM, Bart RM, Ashley RL, Velasco T, Wise SR. An Overview of Blood Flow Restriction Physiology and Clinical Considerations. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2022;21(4):123-128.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000000948",
   "abstract":"Blood flow restriction (BFR) has attracted attention for strength enhancement, muscle hypertrophy and improved function in specific populations. BFR creates a hypoxic environment within a muscle group that stimulates protein synthesis, satellite cell gene regulation and fibre recruitment. Consideration of the individual patient, occlusion pressure, cuff width and cuff size is paramount. BFR is described as consistently safe and effective for augmenting rehabilitation of the upper and lower extremities.",
   "tldr":"Low-load BFR can build strength and muscle in rehabilitation when cuff pressure is set as a percentage of occlusion pressure and the athlete is screened. It gives smaller strength gains than heavy loading, so it is a substitute only when heavy loads are not tolerated.",
   "methods":"A narrative overview of BFR physiology (metabolic stress, mechanical tension, cell swelling, cardiovascular responses, hyperemia), protocol choices (occlusion pressure, cuff width and material, load selection), alternative uses (passive BFR, aerobic BFR, older adults) and safety (VTE, rhabdomyolysis, oxidative stress, numbness). The paper describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria.",
   "findings":"Low-load BFR (about 30% of 1RM) produced hypertrophy and strength gains, and a meta-analysis found greater strength gains than repetition-matched low-load training but less than heavy training. An occlusion pressure of about 40% of arterial occlusion pressure was suggested, and higher pressures did not improve outcomes. In a survey of 250 practitioners, 43.4% used preassigned pressures and 11.5% used a percentage of occlusion pressure. Submaximal low-load BFR caused little muscle damage, and a reported Kaatsu VTE incidence of 0.06% was below the general population rate in Japan. Rhabdomyolysis estimates differed between authors (0.07% to 0.2% vs 0.008% in Japan).",
   "limitations":"The paper is a narrative overview with no search method, so study selection cannot be judged. Protocols and cuff methods varied across the cited studies, and the authors state that mechanisms are not fully understood and that more research is needed on the contribution of each pathway. Safety statements depend on incidence figures from one country and on disputed rhabdomyolysis estimates.",
   "practicalImplications":"When heavy loading is not tolerated during rehabilitation, low-load BFR at about 30% of 1RM with cuff pressure set as a percentage of occlusion pressure (around 40%) may be used under screening, with cuff width and size matched to the limb. Screen for the listed contraindications and VTE risk factors first, and avoid taking low-load BFR to failure, given the damage concerns raised.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited but relevant. The review reports strength and hypertrophy gains with low-load BFR, aerobic gains with BFR walking or cycling, and smaller strength gains than heavy loading. Athlete performance benefits are not tested in trained athletes, so the paper supports BFR as a supplement when heavy loading is limited, not as a replacement for heavy training.",
   "rtp":"Relevant to rehabilitation, where the review describes BFR as an option for postoperative and injured patients who cannot tolerate heavy loads. It does not give return-to-sport criteria or timing, and it cannot be used to show that BFR shortens return to sport."
 }
}

Check, in order:
1. **Identity:** is the text really the article the `sourceFile` name describes? If not, the decision must be EXCLUDE (identity mismatch).
2. **Decision:** is it correct under the INSTRUCTIONS eligibility rules? Narrative reviews, case reports and validation studies are eligible. Editorials and commentaries are not.
3. **DOI:** is it the article's own DOI, printed in the text, and not taken from the references? If no own DOI is printed, the decision is DEGRADED with `doiMissing: true` and a `degradedReason`.
4. **Metadata:** year (journal issue year), citation details actually printed in the text, studyDesign, primaryDomain, and the populations, sex and health-status tags.
5. **Every factual claim** in every text field: sample sizes, design, effects, directions, significance, within-group vs between-group, causal language, and practical advice that the findings do not support.

**Fix problems directly.** Write the corrected full record to `verified/<ID>.json`, using the same schema as the draft plus:
```
"verification": {
  "status": "VERIFIED|CORRECTED|DECISION_CHANGED",
  "changes": ["field: what was wrong -> what it is now (brief source quote)"],
  "residualConcerns": "anything a human reviewer should look at, or empty",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high|normal"
}
```
Set `spotCheckPriority: "high"` when you changed the decision, made a substantive claim correction, the paper is clinically sensitive (concussion, cardiac, medication, return-to-play clearance), or residual concerns remain.

Keep the house style: 1-3 plain sentences per field, no em dashes, no generic advice. Do not rewrite fields that are already accurate.

Omit placeholder citation strings (for example `2018;0:1-9`, `0(0)`, `Vol 00`). Write only to `verified/<ID>.json` and your own `helpers/<your-folder>/`.

   "doi":"10.31236/osf.io/nhqbx",
   "abstract":"Objective: To investigate whether the relationship between the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and health problems varies when different methodological approaches are used. Design: Prospective cohort study. Methods: An online questionnaire collected daily health and training data from 86 elite youth footballers for 105 days. ACWR was calculated with 21- and 28-day chronic periods, coupled and uncoupled, exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) and rolling average, and categorized by pre-defined bins and z-scores; three outcomes were tested in 108 random-effects logistic regression analyses. Results: 6250 training days and 196 health problems were recorded; 24 (22%) of 108 analyses were significant. Conclusions: The relationship between ACWR and health problems depends on methodological choices.",
   "tldr":"In 86 elite youth footballers, 22% of 108 ACWR analysis variants showed a significant link to health problems, and the result depended on how ACWR was calculated and analysed. Treat any single reported ACWR association with caution.",
   "methods":"A prospective cohort of six elite U-19 Norwegian football teams (three girls' and three boys') ran from July to October 2017, covering summer break and 13 to 14 weeks of in-season competition. Players reported daily session duration and RPE by online questionnaire (training load in arbitrary units = duration times RPE) and new or worsening health problems, which a clinician then classified using UEFA guidelines by telephone interview. Twelve ACWR variants were tested against three outcomes (all health problems, all injuries, new non-contact injuries), giving 108 random-effects logistic regression analyses that were not adjusted for sex, age or clustering.",
   "findings":"Of 108 analyses, 24 (22%) were significant. Significant results were most often EWMA-based (15 of 24) and in low-versus-high comparisons (12 of 36, 33%). Incidence was 42.0 health problems, 19.4 injuries and 9.63 new non-contact injuries per 1000 hours. The largest odds ratio reported in the figure was 5.28 (95% CI 1.83-15.25) for a non-coupled 7:28-day rolling-average z-score ACWR comparing low with high categories, for all injuries.",
   "limitations":"Health problems were self-reported and not medically confirmed, 31% of daily questionnaires were unanswered, and the post-study survey found under-reporting. Several Discussion figures conflict with Table 2, including all health problems (31% in the table vs 33% in the abstract), new non-contact injuries (6% vs 2%), 28-day vs 21-day periods (15% vs 26% significant, the reverse of the text), and coupled vs non-coupled (21% vs 19%); table values are reported here. The text describes the strongest association as coupled 7:21 EWMA (OR 5.27), which does not match the figure, and the PDF prints no publication year, so 2020 comes from the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff reading ACWR studies should ask whether all analyses were reported and how ACWR was calculated before trusting a single significant result. When collecting data for youth squads, the paper supports recording all health complaints, not only time-loss injuries, but it does not support using ACWR thresholds to manage load.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited. The study does not test whether ACWR-guided load changes improve performance. Its relevance is that calculation choices (period length, rolling average vs EWMA, categories) change the reported load-health picture, so ACWR bands should not be used as fixed training prescriptions.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable as a return-to-sport study. It reports health problems across a season, not return-to-play decisions, so it cannot be used to decide how quickly a returning player can increase training load."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"A narrative review of accelerometer-based load metrics (PlayerLoad, Body Load, Dynamic Stress Load) from upper back-mounted GNSS units in team sports. The authors report that reliability is mostly high to very high with good coefficients of variation for many outputs, while validity against motion capture and ground reaction force varies with filtering, device and activity. Links to internal load and injury are mixed, with one rugby league study finding only a moderate association between 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation and injury probability.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Most validity and reliability data come from single devices, specific filters and short activity protocols, and the authors note that internal biomechanical load is rarely measured.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may treat PlayerLoad or Dynamic Stress Load as valid measures of tissue load or injury risk, when the review finds the injury and internal-load links are weak or mixed and the metrics are not comparable across devices, manufacturers or athletes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Dawson L, Beato M, Devereux G, McErlain-Naylor SA. A Review of the Validity and Reliability of Accelerometer-Based Metrics From Upper Back-Mounted GNSS Player Tracking Systems for Athlete Training Load Monitoring. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(8):e460-e475.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004835",
   "abstract":"Athlete load monitoring with upper back-mounted GNSS player tracking is common in team sports, and accelerometer-based metrics may add information that GNSS alone cannot provide. This review appraises the validity and reliability of these accelerometers and their metrics (for example PlayerLoad, Dynamic Stress Load and Body Load). Reliability depends on equipment model, signal processing and activity. Upper back placement may be suboptimal for estimating mechanical load. Validity has mostly been judged against other load and intensity measures, with correlations that vary in size and certainty. Metrics should not be compared between athletes or manufacturers, and further study is needed on links to biomechanical load pathways.",
   "tldr":"Upper back-mounted GNSS accelerometer metrics are generally reliable within the same device, but their validity depends on filtering, device and activity. Do not compare them between athletes or manufacturers.",
   "methods":"A narrative review of accelerometer-based metrics from upper back-mounted GNSS units in team sports. The authors describe the published equations for PlayerLoad, Body Load (including the New Body Load variant) and Dynamic Stress Load, then tabulate validity studies against motion capture and ground reaction force (raw and filtered data) and reliability studies (CV and ICC). The paper describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria.",
   "findings":"Reliability of GNSS-housed accelerometer data and metrics is largely high to very high, with mostly good CVs, though some studies show only moderate correlations and moderate to poor CVs. Raw signals are generally less valid than filtered signals; a complementary filter, or filtering at 20 Hz for high-impact and 10 Hz for lower-impact activity, improves agreement with motion capture. Metrics correlate moderately to very highly with distance, speed and some internal load measures (heart rate, session RPE), but correlations with blood lactate are low or negligible. In rugby league, a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation had a moderate association with injury probability (AUC 0.585, 95% CI 0.482-0.672), while 2- and 3-week accumulations did not.",
   "limitations":"The review describes no search method or inclusion criteria, so study selection cannot be judged. The authors note that validity depends on manufacturer, processing, filtering and activity, that vertical acceleration can mask collision accelerations in rugby, and that links to internal biomechanical load are rarely studied. Upper back placement may be suboptimal for estimating whole-body mechanical load.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the same device for repeated comparisons, and avoid comparing athletes or manufacturers directly. Set filtering and the size of a meaningful change using the reported CVs and check that the metric fits the activity, such as using PlayerLoadSlow or a 2D Body Load for rugby collisions. Do not treat these metrics as measures of tissue load or injury risk on the strength of this review.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review supports within-device, within-athlete trend monitoring of acceleration load across training, including sprint and change-of-direction demands, because metrics track running speed and direction changes. It does not support comparing athletes or manufacturers, and it does not show that any metric guides training design.",
   "rtp":"Limited. The review reports one rugby league association between a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation and injury probability (moderate AUC), and notes that both increased and decreased values have been linked to injury risk. It cannot be used to set return-to-play load thresholds or judge tissue readiness."
 }

   "doi":"10.1111/sms.14326",
   "abstract":"Purpose: to assess activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running, comparing within and between muscle activity, relative contribution, and hip and knee angles at peak activity. Methods: multichannel EMG of male basketball players on a treadmill at 15 locations (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus). Results: 29 non-injured players (mean age 17 years). Heterogeneous activity was found within every hamstring muscle; in late swing, semimembranosus activity and relative contribution were higher than semitendinosus. Hip and knee angles at peak activity did not differ. Conclusion: hamstrings were most active in late swing, with the semimembranosus most active and the semitendinosus least active; the most proximal biceps femoris long head region was more active in late swing, and peak activity occurred at similar joint angles.",
   "tldr":"In uninjured male basketball players sprinting on a treadmill, hamstring activity was uneven within each muscle, peaked in late swing, and was lowest in the semitendinosus. Use this as a description of normal activation, not a measure of injury risk.",
   "methods":"A sub-study of an RCT (NL7248) in male basketball players aged 16 or older without hamstring injury in the prior 12 months. Fifteen surface EMG electrode pairs (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus) were placed on the left leg and normalized to three MVICs. Motion capture (100 Hz) defined early-swing, late-swing and stance phases in three strides at the highest maintained treadmill speed. Activity was tested with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping and repeated-measures ANOVA, and joint angles at peak activity with repeated-measures ANOVA.",
   "findings":"Of 38 participants tested, 29 were analysed. Within biceps femoris long head, the most proximal electrode had higher activity than all other locations (F(4,112) = 4.68). Between muscles, semitendinosus was lower than biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus in early swing and lower than semimembranosus in late swing (F(2,56) = 7.31). Relative contribution of semitendinosus was lower than the other two muscles in early and late swing (F(2,56) = 7.28). All peak activity occurred in late swing at mean hip 65.4 degrees and knee 57.3 degrees, with no significant differences in joint angle between muscles or locations.",
   "limitations":"Only uninjured players were tested, so findings may not transfer to injured athletes, and two participants had prior ACL injuries (one with semitendinosus graft). Surface EMG cross-talk cannot be fully excluded, a single MVIC was used for normalization, and the harness and recording device added about 4 kg. Treadmill running was used, and the authors note that the late-swing difference in normalized activity disappeared when electrodes were placed by SENIAM rather than by multichannel selection. The PDF prints no journal name or issue year, so 2023 comes from the Crossref record and the download stamp.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff screening or rehabilitating hamstrings may note that late swing is the phase of highest activity in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, and that the proximal biceps femoris long head is most active there. The study does not test whether injury-prevention or rehabilitation exercises change this distribution, so it should not be used to select exercises on its own.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited. The study describes muscle activation in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, but it does not test whether training changes activation or improves sprint performance. It supports understanding how the hamstrings share load during sprinting, not prescribing a load.",
   "rtp":"Limited. Because only uninjured players were studied, the paper cannot set return-to-running or hamstring readiness criteria, and it does not show that activation patterns after injury return to normal. It may inform future studies that compare activation in injured and uninjured athletes."

lines: "abstract":"Acupuncture and dry needling share mechanisms and sports medicine applications. Pain is the most common indication, but there are limited studies on ergogenic use. content.content:
Q01 findings : Ten studies were included (9 NCAA, 1 U Sports; 319 participants, 14.1% female). Seven studies examined training load and three examined fatigue. In a tackle football study, injury risk was higher when the acute to chronic workload ratio was 2 SD above or below the individual mean, and greatest at 2 SD above (Sampson et al.). In a basketball cohort of 19 athletes, sleep duration and muscle soreness were significant predictors of injury (Watson et al.). The authors found no study that examined mental health as a predictor of sport injury in university sport. 

Q01 limitations : The authors note inconsistent injury surveillance, no control for athlete exposure, no sex- or gender-based analysis, and limited consideration of performance level. Training load was often used as a proxy for tissue load. Most included studies were NCAA football, two studies were female-only, and the fatigue theme mostly measured throwing kinematics rather than injury. The model was not validated against data. 

Q04 methods : Following PRISMA, the authors searched PubMed and SPORTDiscus up to 1 July 2023 using GNSS, GPS, accelerometer and IMU terms with sprinting, team sports and athletes, plus reference lists. Eligible studies were concurrent validity or reliability studies of GNSS linear sprint outputs in athletes, in English and peer reviewed; the protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework. Study quality used a modified Downs and Black checklist. A mixed-effects meta-analysis of radar or laser criterion studies pooled SMDs, with moderator analyses for sampling rate (10 Hz or more vs under 10 Hz) and manufacturer. 

Q04 findings : Sixteen studies were included, most with radar or laser criteria. Pooled SMDs were small for maximal sprint speed (d = 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.42, I2 = 55%), t (d = -0.18, 95% CI -0.60 to 0.23, I2 = 87%), V0 (d = 0.14), relative F0 (d = 0.15) and relative Pmax (d = 0.21). Sampling rates under 10 Hz and some manufacturers showed moderate overestimation of speed, and CVs were under 5% for MSS, V0 and relative Pmax but over 5% for F0 and t. The authors describe visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger tests as showing no publication bias. 

Q04 limitations : The meta-analysis includes only radar and laser criteria, and many studies used small samples, filtered or raw data inconsistently, and under-reported filter settings. Several included studies used timing gates as the criterion, which the authors say may not suit acceleration-based comparisons. Only two databases were searched. The year 2023 is as printed in the PDF; the Crossref record gives 2024, so the PDF year is used. 

Q05 methods : A sub-study of an RCT (NL7248) in male basketball players aged 16 or older without hamstring injury in the prior 12 months. Fifteen surface EMG electrode pairs (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus) were placed on the left leg and normalized to three MVICs. Motion capture (100 Hz) defined early-swing, late-swing and stance phases in three strides at the highest maintained treadmill speed. Activity was tested with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping and repeated-measures ANOVA, and joint angles at peak activity with repeated-measures ANOVA. 

Q05 findings : Of 38 participants tested, 29 were analysed. Within biceps femoris long head, the most proximal electrode had higher activity than all other locations (F(4,112) = 4.68). Between muscles, semitendinosus was lower than biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus in early swing and lower than semimembranosus in late swing (F(2,56) = 7.31). Relative contribution of semitendinosus was lower than the other two muscles in early and late swing (F(2,56) = 7.28). All peak activity occurred in late swing at mean hip 65.4 degrees and knee 57.3 degrees, with no significant differences in joint angle between muscles or locations. 

Q05 limitations : Only uninjured players were tested, so findings may not transfer to injured athletes, and two participants had prior ACL injuries (one with semitendinosus graft). Surface EMG cross-talk cannot be fully excluded, a single MVIC was used for normalization, and the harness and recording device added about 4 kg. Treadmill running was used, and the authors note that the late-swing difference in normalized activity disappeared when electrodes were placed by SENIAM rather than by multichannel selection. The PDF prints no journal name or issue year, so 2023 comes from the Crossref record and the download stamp.

 "evidenceSummary":"A descriptive multichannel surface EMG study of 29 uninjured male basketball players (mean age 17, maximal running speed 7.6 ± 0.5 m/s) running on a treadmill, with 15 electrode pairs over the three hamstring muscles.  "screeningLimitations":"Only uninjured male basketball players were studied, on a treadmill, with a single MVIC-based normalization and surface EMG that is vulnerable to cross-talk. The study measures activation pattern, not injury risk or load, so it cannot show why hamstring injuries occur.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may read the late-swing activity pattern as evidence of the injury mechanism or as proof that a specific hamstring exercise changes load sharing, when the study only describes activation in uninjured players at one running speed.",
 "paper":{

   "citation":"Suskens JJM, Tol JL, Kerkhoffs GMMJ, Maas H, van Dieën JH, Reurink G. Activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running: a descriptive multichannel surface EMG study. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1111/sms.14326",
   "abstract":"Purpose: to assess activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running, comparing within and between muscle activity, relative contribution, and hip and knee angles at peak activity. Methods: multichannel EMG of male basketball players on a treadmill at 15 locations (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus). Results: 29 non-injured players (mean age 17 years). Heterogeneous activity was found within every hamstring muscle; in late swing, semimembranosus activity and relative contribution were higher than semitendinosus. Hip and knee angles at peak activity did not differ. Conclusion: hamstrings were most active in late swing, with the semimembranosus most active and the semitendinosus least active; the most proximal biceps femoris long head region was more active in late swing, and peak activity occurred at similar joint angles.",
   "tldr":"In uninjured male basketball players sprinting on a treadmill, hamstring activity was uneven within each muscle, peaked in late swing, and was lowest in the semitendinosus. Use this as a description of normal activation, not a measure of injury risk.",
   "methods":"A sub-study of an RCT (NL7248) in male basketball players aged 16 or older without hamstring injury in the prior 12 months. Fifteen surface EMG electrode pairs (five biceps femoris long head, four semitendinosus, six semimembranosus) were placed on the left leg and normalized to three MVICs. Motion capture (100 Hz) defined early-swing, late-swing and stance phases in three strides at the highest maintained treadmill speed. Activity was tested with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping and repeated-measures ANOVA, and joint angles at peak activity with repeated-measures ANOVA.",
   "findings":"Of 38 participants tested, 29 were analysed. Within biceps femoris long head, the most proximal electrode had higher activity than all other locations (F(4,112) = 4.68). Between muscles, semitendinosus was lower than biceps femoris long head and semimembranosus in early swing and lower than semimembranosus in late swing (F(2,56) = 7.31). Relative contribution of semitendinosus was lower than the other two muscles in early and late swing (F(2,56) = 7.28). All peak activity occurred in late swing at mean hip 65.4 degrees and knee 57.3 degrees, with no significant differences in joint angle between muscles or locations.",
   "limitations":"Only uninjured players were tested, so findings may not transfer to injured athletes, and two participants had prior ACL injuries (one with semitendinosus graft). Surface EMG cross-talk cannot be fully excluded, a single MVIC was used for normalization, and the harness and recording device added about 4 kg. Treadmill running was used, and the authors note that the late-swing difference in normalized activity disappeared when electrodes were placed by SENIAM rather than by multichannel selection. The PDF prints no journal name or issue year, so 2023 comes from the Crossref record and the download stamp.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff screening or rehabilitating hamstrings may note that late swing is the phase of highest activity in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, and that the proximal biceps femoris long head is most active there. The study does not test whether injury-prevention or rehabilitation exercises change this distribution, so it should not be used to select exercises on its own.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited. The study describes muscle activation in uninjured players at near-maximal running speed, but it does not test whether training changes activation or improves sprint performance. It supports understanding how the hamstrings share load during sprinting, not prescribing a load.",
   "rtp":"Limited. Because only uninjured players were studied, the paper cannot set return-to-running or hamstring readiness criteria, and it does not show that activation patterns after injury return to normal. It may inform future studies that compare activation in injured and uninjured athletes."
 }
}
